Docusign Envelope ID: 081F4975-91DF-4C41-9C19-848E9D73C148




                                                       PROJECT NO. 58481

              RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                         § PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
              LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                      §
              STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561                   §            OF TEXAS


                              COMMENTS OF PRIORITY POWER MANAGEMENT LLC
                                      ON STAFF DISCUSSION DRAFT
                                    NEW 16 TAC §25.194 AND QUESTIONS

                     COMES NOW Priority Power Management LLC (PPM) and files these comments

             regarding Commission Staff’s Discussion Draft proposing a new 16 Texas Administrative Code

             (TAC) §25.194 relating to Large Load Interconnection Standards, which would set forth the

             standards and criteria for an electric utility to interconnect a large load customer to the ERCOT

             transmission network. PPM is also providing comments in response to Commission Staff’s

             Questions posed with the Discussion Draft. Commission Staff requested comments be filed by

             December 19, 2025, so these comments are timely filed.

                     PPM is a North America energy services firm that supports large commercial, industrial,

             and public-sector customers with powered land development, private energy infrastructure

             solutions, microgrid and behind-the-meter solutions, energy procurement, and ongoing market and

             operational management. Priority Power delivers generation- and load-side solutions for

             customers—including mission-critical facilities—to ensure reliable power and enable long-term

             growth.

                     PPM appreciates the opportunity to file comments on Staff’s Discussion Draft and

             Questions. We note that developing a rule that establishes appropriate and necessary standards and

             processes for large load interconnection requires a delicate balance. Staff’s Discussion Draft

             provides a solid foundation, and our comments are aimed at improving clarity to the extent

             possible.
 Docusign Envelope ID: 081F4975-91DF-4C41-9C19-848E9D73C148




                                       RESPONSES TO COMMISSION QUESTIONS

             1.      Should the commission define parameters for determining whether a large load
                     customer is pursuing a substantially similar interconnection request? If so, how
                     should the commission define those parameters?

                     Yes. Additional clarity is needed to determine when a second interconnection request

             would qualify as “substantially similar.” Critical to the definition is the draft language that Staff

             has proposed in subsection (c)(3), (e)(3), and (h)(3) stating that a “substantially similar” project is

             one where “approval of which would result in the customer materially changing, delaying, or

             withdrawing the interconnection request.” Stated differently, if a requesting party could execute

             on both requests, they should not have to disclose the projects as being “substantially similar.”

             Given that withdrawal of a request has a clear meaning, PPM suggests that additional clarification

             could be made by stating more clearly what would constitute a “material” change or delay in a

             project. For example, a one-year delay on a project should be considered material. Other material

             changes would include a 20% change in project capacity or a change in the location for the point

             of interconnection.

             2.      Proposed subsections (c)(3), (e)(3), and (h)(3) require the disclosure of specific
                     information related to a substantially similar request for interconnection and allows
                     a large load customer to anonymize competitively sensitive details. Should the
                     commission list what is and is not competitively sensitive (e.g., load zone is not
                     competitively sensitive information)? If so, what information should and should not
                     be considered competitively sensitive such that the interconnecting utility and
                     ERCOT can identify whether there is a duplicate request, or a request is unlikely to
                     materialize?

                     PPM agrees that the rule language would benefit from additional specificity regarding what

             is and is not competitively sensitive. Rule provisions should be clarified in a consistent manner to

             specify the information that must be disclosed, what information and data can be anonymized, as

             well as what information and data cannot be withheld. PPM agrees that load zone should not be

             considered competitively sensitive. ERCOT Protocol Section 3.2.7, Large Load Interconnection


                                         Priority Power Comments on Staff Discussion Draft 16 TAC §25.194 – Page 2
 Docusign Envelope ID: 081F4975-91DF-4C41-9C19-848E9D73C148




             Status Report, provides a list of data that ERCOT must include in its monthly Status Report. Since

             ERCOT will need to collect the underlying information from TSPs, each TSP should receive this

             information from a large load customer that is requesting interconnection, but the information may

             nonetheless remain protected from disclosure to the public.

             3.      Should the commission require a large load customer to notify the interconnecting
                     electric utility and ERCOT of any change to information that is initially disclosed in
                     response to this rule or only material changes to the information disclosed? If only
                     material changes, how should “material change” be defined?

                     PPM recommends that the Commission require a large load customer to notify the utility

             only about material changes to the information initially disclosed. We agree additional clarity is

             needed to define “material change.” See response to Question No. 1 for examples of what would

             constitute a material change.

             4.      Proposed subsection (k)(1) authorizes an interconnecting electric utility to refund
                     20% of a large load customer's security after energization and ratably as the large
                     load customer meets the milestones identified in the customer’s schedule for phased
                     energization of its contracted load. Should the commission standardize the rate for
                     refund for reaching milestones identified in the customer’s schedule for phased
                     energization (e.g., 20% for each year of operations until the full amount of security is
                     refunded)? If so, how should the commission standardize the refund?

                     A “ratable” refund is generally understood to be a pro rata refund of the unused portion of

             security deposit. PPM agrees that the rule would benefit from additional clarity regarding the

             schedule for the rate of refund and further agrees that such refund schedule should be standardized.

             However, the timing for the refund also will depend, as discussed below regarding proposed

             subsection (c)(8), on the clear identification of the purpose of the $50,000/MW financial security

             when the large load customer has already paid a study fee (or fees) to cover the costs for the

             interconnecting electric utility and ERCOT to study the interconnection and also will be required

             to pay Cost in Aid of Construction (CIAC) before the interconnecting electric utility begins

             construction of the interconnection. If neither of these expenses are paid, then the large load


                                         Priority Power Comments on Staff Discussion Draft 16 TAC §25.194 – Page 3
 Docusign Envelope ID: 081F4975-91DF-4C41-9C19-848E9D73C148




             customer will not be interconnected, and there will be no need for this financial security to be

             posted. If both of these fees and CIAC are paid, it is not clear what additional interconnection

             expenses might be deducted from the $50,000/MW financial security. If there are such costs, the

             rule should clearly identify them. Once the identified costs that are secured by this financial

             security have been paid, there should be no need for the interconnecting electric utility to retain

             this financial security, and a prompt refund, rather than a multi-year process, would be appropriate.

                     To the extent that there is a quantifiable need for this security to be held to secure costs that

             the large load customer has not paid but may become due over an extended period of time, and

             there is a need to retain a reduced amount of security over that time, then a pro rata return of the

             security could be appropriate, PPM suggests there are two ways that the pro rata refund could be

             accomplished over the five year period: 1) based on percentage of the contracted peak demand that

             has been energized; or 2) based on a linear ramp over time, i.e., X% per year where X is the same

             amount each year, such as 20% per year over five years. PPM suggests that both options be

             included in the rule, with the default being a set percentage released annually as a linear ramp, but

             giving the requesting party the option to select a refund schedule proportional to the percentage of

             contracted peak demand if the ramp rate for phasing in the energization would exceed the

             percentages in the default schedule. See comments on subsection (k)(1) for specific rule language,

             where PPM proposes these options and addresses additional ambiguities in Staff’s draft language.

             5.      Are changes to the commission’s other substantive rules necessary to align with this
                     rulemaking? If so, what changes need to be made to which rules?

                     No comment at this time.


                                    COMMENTS ON PROPOSED RULE LANGUAGE

                     PPM provides the following comments on specific provisions of the discussion draft rule

             language. Proposed amendments are offered as a redline to the Staff Discussion draft.

                                         Priority Power Comments on Staff Discussion Draft 16 TAC §25.194 – Page 4
 Docusign Envelope ID: 081F4975-91DF-4C41-9C19-848E9D73C148




             Subsection (b), Definitions.

                     Subsection (b)(3) includes a typographical error, referencing subsection (d) when it should

             reference (e) (Discretionary Services Agreement). This language should be corrected as follows:

                     (3)      Discretionary services agreement – An agreement, executed and securitized by a
                              large load customer and interconnecting electric utility after the interconnecting
                              electric utility completes the large load interconnection study and before the
                              interconnecting electric utility submits the study to ERCOT, that, at a minimum,
                              satisfies subsection (ed) of this section.

                     Subsection (b)(7) defines Large Load Customer and measures the customer’s total peak

             demand “at a single site”. In the case of midstream oil and gas facilities, there may be multiple

             meters or distributed equipment where there is no individual component that has a peak demand

             that is equal to or exceeds 75 MW, but as these components are installed over time and if they are

             netted, they could equal or exceed that threshold. In these instances, the customer will not have

             requested permission to interconnect the full 75 MW or more of load at the outset. PPM does not

             anticipate that the Commission intends these gradually growing operations to be subject to the

             requirements of the proposed rule. To provide further clarity to the rule, the Commission should

             clarify that a single site includes the load interconnected through the same Facilities Extension

             Agreement (FEA). For example, this definition could be revised as follows:

                     (7)      Large load customer -- A customer requesting a new or expanded
                              interconnection where the customer’s contracted total peak demand at a
                              single site that is interconnected to the electric grid through the same
                              facilities extension agreement and is reasonably forecast for interconnection
                              studies to equal to or exceed exceeds 75 megawatts (MW).

             Subsection (e), Discretionary Services Agreement.

                     In subsection (e)(4) (as well as (h)(4)), the discussion draft requires a large load customer

             to submit to the interconnecting electric utility the large load customer’s plans, expected timing,

             and progress for site-related studies and engineering services required for project development and



                                         Priority Power Comments on Staff Discussion Draft 16 TAC §25.194 – Page 5
 Docusign Envelope ID: 081F4975-91DF-4C41-9C19-848E9D73C148




             to provide to the utility updates or progress reports when requested. While this information may

             be of interest to an electric utility to understanding the customer’s development progress, this

             information is not required to be provided pursuant to PURA §37.0561 and is not relevant to the

             reliable operations of the electric grid. Any reliance on this information as a basis for consideration

             of the customer’s interconnection request could inject subjectivity into the interconnection process.

             As a result, PPM recommends that subsections (e)(4) and (h)(4) be deleted.

                     As we understand the language in the prior subsections (c) and (d), the proposed process

             would be as follows: 1) Customer submits disclosures and pays the study fee to the interconnecting

             electric utility; 2) the electric utility has 30 days to start the interconnection study; and 3) before

             submitting the electric utility’s study to ERCOT, the customer must execute and securitize the

             Discretionary Services Agreement (DSA). Subsection (e)(8) requires a large load customer to pay

             the utility a deposit of $50,000 per MW of contracted peak demand concurrently with execution

             of the DSA. PPM has several concerns with the Staff’s proposed language in this subsection,

             primarily related to the timing and magnitude of the security required. At the outset, it should be

             noted that PURA §37.0561(h) requires the Commission’s rules to “provide satisfactory proof of

             financial commitment”, but does not mandate every form of financial security proposed in this

             discussion draft be mandated. In other words, Senate Bill 6 provides the Commission flexibility

             in this regard.

                     Because the $50,000/MW deposit is a proposed requirement that must be met in order for

             the large load customer to execute a DSA, the customer will be obligated to post security before

             ERCOT reviews anything and while uncertainty is highest regarding viability for the project. This

             timing would force a major capital commitment before ERCOT validates the electric utility’s

             study. In the case of an existing large load customer that already has a Discretionary Services



                                         Priority Power Comments on Staff Discussion Draft 16 TAC §25.194 – Page 6
 Docusign Envelope ID: 081F4975-91DF-4C41-9C19-848E9D73C148




             Agreement (DSA) or Facilities Extension Agreement (FEA), the customer should not be required

             to post $50,000/MW for capacity that is already contracted and secured. The $50,000/MW

             requirement should only apply to incremental MWs above the customer’s existing DSA or FEA.

             This would align the rule with its stated purpose of discouraging speculative requests, and not

             penalizing real, already-secured load.

                     PPM also objects to the magnitude of the security requirement of $50,000/MW because it

             appears to be arbitrary and excessively high for early-stage development, especially considering

             that these requirements will apply to the proposed interconnection of any large load customer,

             including in the oil and gas market or other manufacturing facilities. Burdensome upfront capital

             requirements shift market power, which may reduce competition, affect development timelines,

             and potentially limit access for emerging industries.

                     Finally, the proposed financial security requirement does not appear intended to cover any

             potential financial obligation that the large load customer may be liable for during the

             interconnection process. It is clear that this financial security requirement may help ensure that a

             large load customer that is seeking an interconnection agreement is not speculative. However,

             once that objective is achieved, unless there are clearly identified potential liabilities that this

             financial security is available to ensure payment of, timely refund or release of the financial

             security should be made, such as when the large load customer provides financial security for

             significant equipment or services and contribution in aid of construction (CIAC) when it executes

             its Intermediate Agreement pursuant to subsection (h), or when the customer energizes and is

             operational. According to proposed subsection (e)(8)(B), the utility is allowed to accept the

             following forms of payment for security: 1) cash collateral, 2) corporate or parental guaranty if the

             guarantor has a credit rating of BBB-/Baa3 or higher, or 3) a letter of credit issued by a bank with



                                         Priority Power Comments on Staff Discussion Draft 16 TAC §25.194 – Page 7
 Docusign Envelope ID: 081F4975-91DF-4C41-9C19-848E9D73C148




             a credit rating of BBB-/Baa3 or higher. In light of the fact that the proposed rule will apply to a

             variety of potential large load customers, PPM respectfully recommends that the Commission

             expand its range of acceptable forms of security to include surety bonds and other commercially

             reasonable instruments that provide equivalent protection to utilities without excluding otherwise

             viable projects. Some examples of other commercially reasonable forms of security that could be

             used include project level escrow accounts, standby letters of credit with broader issuer criteria,

             and affiliate guarantees,

                     Finally, PPM recommends that the rule be clarified regarding how the utilities will handle

             interest on cash collateral held as financial security pursuant to subsection (e)(8)(B)(i). The

             financial security that would be required pursuant to this subsection does not appear to be within

             the scope of existing 16 TAC §25.195, Terms and Conditions for Transmission Service, in which

             subsection (e) requires in relevant part, “interest at a commercially reasonable rate based on that

             portion of the deposit being returned.” As a result, this rule should specify the interest rate that

             will be paid on security deposits made by large load customers, the process of accounting for

             interest should be transparent, and there should be clear requirements for the timely return of such

             collateral after the costs that the collateral is securing payment of have been paid.

             Subsection (h), Intermediate agreement.

                     Subsections (c)(1), (e)(1), and (h)(1) each require a statement regarding whether the large

             load requesting interconnection is a developer or an end-use customer. Additionally, in subsection

             (h)(1), if the customer is a developer, it must disclose whether the developer has contracted with a

             tenant for off-take of the service. However, it is not clear the purpose of this additional information

             at this point in the development process. If the Commission intends there to be any specific




                                         Priority Power Comments on Staff Discussion Draft 16 TAC §25.194 – Page 8
 Docusign Envelope ID: 081F4975-91DF-4C41-9C19-848E9D73C148




             consequences if a tenant is not yet contracted to take service at the location at issue, the rule should

             provide such additional clarity.

                     Regarding site control in subsection (h)(2), PPM recommends that the language mirror the

             site control language in subsection (c)(2). It is not clear why a more limited demonstration of site

             control is required at this point.

                     For the reasons discussed above regarding subsection (e)(4), PMM recommends subsection

             (h)(4) be deleted.

                     Regarding subsection (h)(8), PPM is concerned that there may be a “double-dip” risk

             related to financial security that must be posted by the large load customer. Specifically, after

             posting financial security to the interconnecting utility $50,000/MW of contracted peak demand

             under subsection (e)(8), the customer must again securitize at the Intermediate Agreement stage

             (post-ERCOT approval), pursuant to proposed subsection (h)(8) by paying “financial security to

             the interconnecting electric utility in an amount equal to the interconnecting electric utility’s

             expected costs for equipment with a lead time of at least six months and services necessary to

             interconnect the large load customer.” In addition, before the interconnecting electric utility will

             begin construction of facilities to interconnect the same customer, “a large load customer must pay

             CAIC in an amount that is equal to the interconnecting utility’s expected costs to interconnect the

             large load customer and that are directly attributable to interconnecting the large load customer.”

             As noted above, based on the discussion draft’s provisions, it does not appear that the early

             $50,000/MW from subsection (e)(8) is credited, applied to CIAC, applied to long-lead equipment

             costs, or otherwise carried forward into the Intermediate Agreement requirements. In other words,

             it is not clear what the purpose of the early $50,000/MW financial security is, much less why it

             should be held even after the customer starts energizing. Without clarification, Staff’s proposed



                                         Priority Power Comments on Staff Discussion Draft 16 TAC §25.194 – Page 9
 Docusign Envelope ID: 081F4975-91DF-4C41-9C19-848E9D73C148




             language creates the risk of stacked, duplicative financial security obligations, potentially tens to

             hundreds of millions of dollars, which could stymie investment by Texas customers desiring to

             interconnect their large loads, affecting oil and gas midstream plants larger than 75 MW, mining

             facilities, manufacturers, and independent data center developers. As PPM recommends above,

             when the large load customer provides financial security for significant equipment or services and

             CIAC when it executes its Intermediate Agreement pursuant to subsection (h), in the absence of

             additional potential expenses that should be secured, the security provided with the execution of a

             DSA should be refunded at this time or, at the latest, when the customer energizes and is

             operational.

                     Subsection (h)(9) addresses CIAC, and the proposed requirements would benefit from

             additional specificity. In particular, PPM strongly recommends that the Commission require

             utilities to itemize costs for CIAC, including any dollars per megawatt allocations, formulas for

             pro-ration, or any upgrade costs that are “directly attributable” to the large load customer.

             Regarding pro-ration, the proposed rule requires pro-rating based on contracted peak demand but

             does not explain how changes in load requests alter allocations or whether refunds will be refunded

             to earlier customers if a new one shares costs. PPM respectfully requests that the Commission

             clarify these details.

                     Finally, regarding the forms of payment for CAIC provided in subsection (h)(9)(D), as

             PPM comments above in regard to subsection (e)(8)(B), requiring a BBB-credit rating requirement

             for a corporate or parental guaranty or line of credit PPM respectfully recommends the

             Commission expand its range of acceptable forms of security to include surety bonds and other

             commercially reasonable instruments that provide equivalent protection to utilities without

             excluding otherwise viable projects. Some examples of other commercially reasonable forms of



                                        Priority Power Comments on Staff Discussion Draft 16 TAC §25.194 – Page 10
 Docusign Envelope ID: 081F4975-91DF-4C41-9C19-848E9D73C148




             security that could be used include project level escrow accounts, standby letters of credit with

             broader issuer criteria, and affiliate guarantees.

             Subsection (i), Withdrawal of all or a portion of requested or contracted peak demand for
                   interconnection.

                     Subsection (i)(3) states that CIAC that a large load customer has paid is not refundable for

             any reason, even if the customer withdraws a portion of its requested peak demand for

             interconnection.     However, if the electric utility reallocates that customer’s capacity to a

             subsequent large load customer, and equipment or services that the original customer paid for

             through CIAC are used to support the interconnection of the subsequent customer, the original

             customer should receive a refund from the electric utility for the cost of that equipment or services,

             and the subsequent customer should be required to pay those CIAC costs to the interconnecting

             electric utility, similar to the concept provided in subsection (h)(9)(C). At a minimum, the

             language should be modified to allow for a refund to a large load customer within 60 days if the

             capacity is reassigned to another customer:

                     (3) CIAC that the large load customer paid is not refundable, unless some or all of the
                         capacity is reassigned to one or more other customers, in which case the utility must
                         refund the CIAC within 60 days of such reassignment.

             Subsection (j), Reallocation of capacity.

                     Subsection (j) requires a utility to reallocate capacity of a large load customer that is

             energized but fails to satisfy, within 18-months, a milestone in its schedule for phased energization

             of the contracted peak demand. PPM recommends modifying the 18-month ramp milestone to

             create additional flexibility for customers. The 18-month ramp as proposed in the Staff Discussion

             Draft does not appear to accommodate certain supply chain limitations or other contingencies that

             are specifically out of the customer’s control, such as transformer failures, in which transformers

             have a 24-36 month (or longer) replacement cycle, non-transformer supply chain delays, or other

                                        Priority Power Comments on Staff Discussion Draft 16 TAC §25.194 – Page 11
 Docusign Envelope ID: 081F4975-91DF-4C41-9C19-848E9D73C148




             engineering, procurement, and construction delays outside a large load customer’s control. At a

             minimum, PPM recommends that the proposed 18-month period be subject to an extension for

             good cause shown. However, due to the significant supply chain issues that the electric industry

             is facing at this time, PPM recommends increasing the 18-month window to a 48-month window,

             plus the opportunity to request a good cause exception for events not tied to over-requesting

             capacity. These changes could be achieved by changing “18” to “48” in the first sentence and by

             adding the following sentence after the first sentence in the Discussion Draft:

                             “The interconnecting electric utility must extend the preceding time to
                     satisfy a milestone to account for contingencies that are out of the large load
                     customer’s control.”

                     Further, PPM requests additional clarification in the rule regarding the process for

             reallocation of capacity. Specifically, PPM requests that the Commission Staff consider questions

             regarding: 1) what is the mechanism by which the large load customer is alerted when contracted

             capacity is reallocated, 2) how any associated financial security will be calculated and refunded,

             and 3) what is the timing for such refunds? PPM recommends that any balances to be refunded be

             returned within 60 days. Additional details surrounding this process may be appropriate for

             stakeholder discussion at a future Commission workshop.

             Subsection (k), Terms for refund of financial security for a large load customer that energizes.

                     As discussed above in PPM’s response to Question No. 4, the timing of a refund to a large

             load customer that energizes depends on the clear identification of the purpose of the $50,000/MW

             financial security. If the large load customer has already paid a study fee (or fees) to cover the

             costs for the interconnecting electric utility and ERCOT to study the interconnection, pays CIAC

             before the interconnecting electric utility begins construction of the interconnection, and now is




                                        Priority Power Comments on Staff Discussion Draft 16 TAC §25.194 – Page 12
 Docusign Envelope ID: 081F4975-91DF-4C41-9C19-848E9D73C148




             energized and operational, there should be no need for the interconnecting electric utility to retain

             this financial security, and a prompt refund, rather than a multi-year process, would be appropriate.

                     To the extent that there is a quantifiable need for this security to be held to secure costs that

             the large load customer has not paid but that may become due, and there is a need to retain at least

             some of the financial security over time, then a pro rata return of the security could be appropriate.

             PPM agrees that the rule would benefit from additional clarity regarding the schedule for the rate

             of refund and further agrees that such refund schedule should be standardized.

                     PPM recommends two ways that the pro rata refund could be accomplished over the five

             year period, for example: 1) based on percentage of the contracted peak demand that has been

             energized; or 2) based on a linear ramp over time, i.e., X% per year where X is the same amount

             each year, such as 20% per year over five years. PPM suggests that both options be included in the

             rule, with the default being a set percentage released annually as a linear ramp, but giving the large

             load customer the option to select a refund schedule proportional to the percentage of contracted

             peak demand if the ramp rate for phasing in the energization would exceed the percentages in the

             default schedule. In either case, the refund of the final balance should not be delayed until the

             customer reaches 100% of its contracted demand. There are a number of reasons why achieving

             100% of the contracted demand may be delayed, and as long as no outstanding potential liabilities

             remain unpaid, the final balance of the refund should be made at an earlier stage, such as when

             80% of the contracted demand has been achieved.

                     As drafted, subsection (k)(2) could be interpreted to mean that the large load customer must

             be operating at peak demand for a full five years before the remaining balance of financial security

             would be refunded, or that the large load customer must have reached its full peak demand after




                                        Priority Power Comments on Staff Discussion Draft 16 TAC §25.194 – Page 13
 Docusign Envelope ID: 081F4975-91DF-4C41-9C19-848E9D73C148




             being operational for five years. To eliminate ambiguity and consistent with PPM’s comments, we

             recommend the following modifications to subsection (k):

                     1.       If there are no remaining costs that require financial security to be retained:

                     (k)      Terms for refund of financial security for a large load customer that
                              energizes. An interconnecting electric utility must apply the financial
                              security that a large load customer paid under this section to any amounts
                              owed for costs incurred by the interconnecting electric utility to fulfill the
                              large load customer’s request for interconnection.
                              (1)     After applying the financial security to any amounts owed, the
                                      interconnecting electric utility must refund 100% 20% of the
                                      remaining balance within 60 days after when the large load customer
                                      energizes and ratably as the large load customer meets the
                                      milestones identified in the customer’ s schedule for phased
                                      energization of its contracted peak demand.

                     2.       If there is a need for a ratable refund:

                     (k)      Terms for refund of financial security for a large load customer that
                              energizes. An interconnecting electric utility must apply the financial
                              security that a large load customer paid under this section to any amounts
                              owed for costs incurred by the interconnecting electric utility to fulfill the
                              large load customer’s request for interconnection.
                              (1)     After applying the financial security to any amounts owed, the
                                      interconnecting electric utility must refund 20% of the remaining
                                      balance when the large load customer energizes, the interconnecting
                                      electric utility must refund 20% of the remaining balance each year
                                      thereafter over a five year period; or and ratably as the large load
                                      customer meets the milestones identified in the customer’ s schedule
                                      for phased energization of its contracted peak demand.
                              (2)     At the customer’s option, if the phased energization of contracted
                                      peak demand would exceed 20% in any year, The interconnecting
                                      electric utility must refund any remaining balance in an amount
                                      corresponding to the percentage of the contracted peak demand
                                      energized each year when the large load sustains operations for five
                                      years at the customer’ s contracted peak demand.




                                        Priority Power Comments on Staff Discussion Draft 16 TAC §25.194 – Page 14
 Docusign Envelope ID: 081F4975-91DF-4C41-9C19-848E9D73C148




                                                             CONCLUSION

                     PPM appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments and encourages the

             Commission to move to formal publication of a proposed rule consistent with these comments.

                                                                    Respectfully submitted,

                                                                    Chief Commercial Officer

                                                       PROJECT NO. 58481

              RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                           § PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
              LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                        §
              STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561                     §            OF TEXAS


                              COMMENTS OF PRIORITY POWER MANAGEMENT LLC
                                      ON STAFF DISCUSSION DRAFT
                                    NEW 16 TAC §25.194 AND QUESTIONS

                                                    EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

             Response to Questions

             Q1: PPM suggests that additional clarification could be made by stating more clearly what would
             constitute a “material” change or delay in a project. For example, a one-year delay on a project
             should be considered material. Other material changes would include a 20% change in project
             capacity or a change in the location for the point of interconnection.

             changes would include a 20% change in project capacity or a change in the location for the point

             of interconnection.

             stakeholder discussion at a future Commission workshop.

             Subsection (k), Terms for refund offinancial security for a large load customer that energizes.

                      As discussed above in PPM's response to Question No. 4, the timing of a refund to a large

             load customer that energizes depends on the clear identification ofthe purpose ofthe $50,000/MW

             financial security. If the large load customer has already paid a study fee (or fees) to cover the

             costs for the interconnecting electric utility and ERCOT to study the interconnection, pays CIAC

             before the interconnecting electric utility begins construction of the interconnection, and now is




                                          Priority Power Comments on Staff Discussion Draft 16 TAC §25.194 - Page 12
 Docusign Envelope ID: 081 F4975-91 DF-4C41-9C1 9-848E9D73C148




             energized and operational, there should be no need for the interconnecting electric utility to retain

             this financial security, and a prompt refund, rather than a multi-year process, would be appropriate.

                      To the extent that there is a quantifiable need for this security to be held to secure costs that

             the large load customer has not paid but that may become due, and there is a need to retain at least

             some of the financial security over time, then a pro rata return of the security could be appropriate.

             PPM agrees that the rule would benefit from additional clarity regarding the schedule for the rate

             of refund and further agrees that such refund schedule should be standardized.

                      PPM recommends two ways that the pro rata refund could be accomplished over the five

             year period, for example: 1) based on percentage of the contracted peak demand that has been

             energized; or 2) based on a linear ramp over time, i.e., X% per year where X is the same amount

             each year, such as 20% per year over five years. PPM suggests that both options be included in the

             rule, with the default being a set percentage released annually as a linear ramp, but giving the large

             load customer the option to select a refund schedule proportional to the percentage of contracted

             peak demand if the ramp rate for phasing in the energization would exceed the percentages in the

             default schedule. In either case, the refund of the final balance should not be delayed until the

             customer reaches 100% of its contracted demand. There are a number of reasons why achieving

             100% of the contracted demand may be delayed, and as long as no outstanding potential liabilities

             remain unpaid, the final balance of the refund should be made at an earlier stage, such as when

             80% of the contracted demand has been achieved.

                      As drafted, subsection (k)(2) could be interpreted to mean that the large load customer must

             be operating at peak demand for a full five years before the remaining balance of financial security

             would be refunded, or that the large load customer must have reached its full peak demand after
